source.title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook

accepted.question_text: For a linear system Ax = b solved by bootstrap algebraic multigrid, what form of compatible relaxation and what convergence-rate estimate derived from the compatible-relaxation factor ρ_cr should be used so that, for a given interpolation strategy, the estimate accurately predicts the convergence of the resulting two-grid method?

evidence.quote: How to define an appropriate form of CR and related convergence rate estimate from ρc r that accurately predicts the performance of the resulting two-grid method for a given interpolation strategy?
However, a precise relation between the convergence rate of a given CR iteration and the resulting two-grid convergence is not known in general.

accepted.question_text: Given a current set C of coarse variables for bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how should one choose the initial coarse set C0 and then make local additions, removals, or other modifications to C whenever compatible relaxation converges too slowly, so that the updated coarse space improves convergence without introducing unnecessary complexity?

evidence.quote: How to choose C0 and how to identify suitable local modifications to a given set of coarse variables whenever the CR convergence rate is slow?

there is still no rigorous understanding of or justification for using pointwise errors of CR to determine the variables that will most effectively reduce the convergence rate of the CR process when added to C.
An efficient mechanism for updating coarse variable set C based on a local slowness of CR relaxation, see Section 2;

accepted.question_text: When least-squares interpolation is built from a finite set of relaxed test vectors, how should one use randomized methods or range-approximation techniques to sample the dominant part of the error space that is not significantly reduced by the smoother, so that the sampled space yields reliably effective interpolation?

evidence.quote: Recently, randomized methods for range approximation have been given particular attention in data mining applications and further studies of the LS process along these lines are still needed.

accepted.question_text: For least-squares interpolation in bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how can one define appropriate local weights ωκ, and possibly corresponding local equations for computing test vectors, in a general algebraic setting so that a globally smooth test vector is not overemphasized in local regions where it has large residuals?

evidence.quote: The related problem of determining appropriate local weights in the LS definition of interpolation is more complicated and has not been resolved in a general algebraic setting, except for finite element discretizations of elliptic boundary value problems.
The problem of determining local weights is also related to the question of deriving local equations for computing the test vectors, as in spectral AMG [22].

A local procedure for finding weights ωκ in (3.1) – to prevent an emphasize on a globally smooth test vector, that will otherwise be heavily weighted everywhere, in the regions where it has large residuals; such approach will be a generalization of the LSR scheme which is now used concurrently with global weights, see Section 3;

accepted.question_text: How should one combine least-squares interpolation, bootstrap setup cycles, and adaptive cycles for computing test vectors in bootstrap algebraic multigrid so that the resulting self-learning setup is both optimal in work and robust across problem classes?

evidence.quote: While this research has resulted in an increased understanding of these techniques, a systematic study of how to combine them in an optimal and robust way is still needed.

accepted.question_text: When computing the test vectors used by bootstrap algebraic multigrid, what balance between computational work and approximation accuracy should be targeted so that the vectors are accurate enough to define effective interpolation without making setup prohibitively expensive?

evidence.quote: A balance between work and accuracy when computing TVs, see Section 4;

accepted.question_text: How can bootstrap algebraic multigrid incorporate all available information about a problem, especially geometric information when it exists, into coarsening, interpolation, and setup so that the resulting multigrid hierarchy uses that information effectively rather than relying only on algebraic heuristics?

evidence.quote: A procedure for incorporating all available information about a given problem, in particular, its geometric information;

accepted.question_text: For general Hermitian positive definite problems, how can the compatible-relaxation, algebraic-distance, least-squares-interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector components of bootstrap algebraic multigrid be integrated into an overall algorithm that is practical, easy to tune, and robust as a fast multigrid solver across a diverse set of test problems, including systems of partial differential equations?

evidence.quote: The main issue to consider in developing BAMG as a fast solver for general HPD problems concerns the integration of the BAMG components in order to obtain an overall algorithm for use in practice.
Specifically, a systematic study of the BAMG processes for a carefully chosen and diverse set of test problems (that includes systems of PDEs) is needed.
An integration of all BAMG components to obtain an easy to tune and robust multigrid solver.

accepted.question_text: For non-Hermitian linear systems, which error components should restriction and interpolation approximate on coarse levels—in other words, how should algebraically smooth error be characterized when the matrix is nonnormal and the near kernel generally cannot be identified just by singular vectors or eigenvectors associated with small singular values?

evidence.quote: One main unresolved issue that arises in a Galerkin-based algebraic multigrid concerns characterizing the algebraically smooth errors that need to be approximated by restriction and interpolation.
Thus, in general the near kernel of the system matrix can not be characterized by the singular vectors (or eigenvectors) with small singular values, unless the matrix is normal.

accepted.question_text: For non-Hermitian problems, how can restriction R and interpolation P be constructed and tied together locally so that the Galerkin coarse-grid matrix remains suitable for multigrid correction and does not become singular or cause divergence through overcorrection when small singular values or eigenvalues are underestimated on coarse levels?

evidence.quote: Thus, it is possible that the Galerkin coarse level operator can have a zero eigenvalue, even when the fine-level matrix does not.
We have observed in practice that in such cases, the resulting Galerkin method can diverge.

Thus, although the BAMG process provides techniques for constructing restriction R and interpolation P, each in their own setup scheme, these processes must be carefully tied together locally in order to obtain a suitable Galerkin coarse-grid matrix.

accepted.question_text: For indefinite or non-elliptic problems such as higher-dimensional Helmholtz and Schrödinger equations, how can one build a bootstrap algebraic multigrid method that uses several prolongation operators and multiple Galerkin coarse-grid operators, with the prolongation operators kept locally orthogonal, so that the many locally different low-eigenspace components are represented accurately at acceptable computational cost?

evidence.quote: The key issues is that such eigenfunctions cannot be accurately interpolated by a single prolongation operator (3.1) with a small caliber, starting with some sufficiently fine scales.
There and on all coarser scales several prolongation operators have to be employed, resulting in multiple-Galerkin approach with many coarse-grid operators.
To guarantee optimal computational costs, all prolongation operators have to be locally orthogonal, and achieving that generates additional computational difficulties.
Two important future research topics are thus to continue to investigate developing BAMG solvers for these and other non-elliptic problems

accepted.question_text: How far can bootstrap algebraic multigrid techniques developed for non-elliptic and other challenging sparse systems be extended so that they become genuinely fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations beyond the problem classes where BAMG-like methods have already been implemented?

evidence.quote: Two important future research topics are thus to continue to investigate developing BAMG solvers for these and other non-elliptic problems and to determine how far these techniques can be extended as fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations.
